### D55: Which workflow and tag release gobby once CP-PREDELETE-CUT's commit B has removed the Python console script? Today a v* tag runs .github/workflows/release.yml: a gate that waits for the CI workflow's run on the tag's commit (the CI workflow also runs on v* tags, .github/workflows/ci.yml:6-8), uv build, the PyPI publish, a GitHub release of dist/* and the gobby-release dispatch to GobbyAI/homebrew-tap (.github/workflows/release.yml:3-158). A gclient-v* tag runs .github/workflows/release-gclient.yml: the client's tests, the crates.io publish and a GitHub release of gclient-<target>.tar.gz marked --latest=false (.github/workflows/release-gclient.yml:8-196). No gclient-v* tag has been pushed yet.
- **resolved_by:** Josh, 2026-11-04 ~14:07 CT, ruling 22
- **status:** Approved as first shown. The later amendment that drops release.yml's manual dispatch comes to Josh with the map.
- **recommended_default:** release-gclient.yml on its gclient-v* tag. Commit B deletes release.yml, which ends the PyPI publish; moves its CI gate (.github/workflows/release.yml:18-38) into release-gclient.yml ahead of the client's publish and release jobs, and its tap dispatch job after the GitHub release, with the version taken from the gclient-v* tag; changes the CI workflow's v* tag trigger to gclient-v*, so the gate finds a CI run of the tagged commit; archives the client binary as gobby in gobby-<target>.tar.gz; and marks the release latest. A v* tag then releases nothing. Outside this repository, GobbyAI/homebrew-tap's gobby formula switches to the client archive before the first gclient-v* tag after commit B and raises its version_scheme, because the client's 0.1.x version (crates/gclient/Cargo.toml:3) is below the last Python release (PyPI 0.4.6; v0.4.9 was tagged but never packaged). S3-DELETE replaces release-gclient.yml's three Python steps (the moved CI gate and the two gobby-terminal preflights) with shell steps. Alternative: make release.yml the gobby release on v* tags, with release-gclient.yml's build matrix, checksums and crates.io publish moved in beside its CI gate, and delete release-gclient.yml at S3-DELETE, whose Python tests pin it until then. Under the default, commit B drops release.yml's manual workflow_dispatch trigger and its gate_only input rather than moving them: every job but the CI gate already requires a push event (.github/workflows/release.yml:7-13, 43, 72, 95, 119), so a dispatch only checks a commit's CI run, and nothing in the repository dispatches it or documents it since docs/releasing.md, added with it in 27460b3f28 (#14821), was removed.
- **rationale:** #21573 names the release workflows and Homebrew in the switch's change set. Keeping the client's own tag and workflow moves two jobs, renames the archives, retargets one CI tag trigger and changes no version line in this repository, and the gobby release keeps its gate on a green CI run for the tagged commit. PyPI's gobby package stays at 0.4.6, its last published release; v0.4.9 was tagged but never packaged. The alternative keeps the v* tag but makes it track gobby-client's Cargo version, which is below the v* tags already pushed, and leaves two workflows building the client until S3-DELETE. Moving the dispatch would need a push-event condition on every job of release-gclient.yml, its tag-version check included, to keep a check that nothing calls.

### D71: How do native agent-run completions reach Python's in-process CompletionEventRegistry before AG-WAIT, and what wakes the native waiters that exist before then? agents-family Decision 15 bridges native completions into the registry through a new Python route, POST /_gobby/agent-run-delivery (agents-family 2.0), which D4 and D19 forbid.
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default.
- **recommended_default:** AG-1 adds the completion hand-off, deliver_completion, to gagents' machine effects (.gobby/plans/agents-family.md Decision 6 and 6.1). gdaemon's implementation keeps an in-memory set of run ids, each with the message its caller composes (src/gobby/mcp_proxy/tools/agent_cancellation.py:113, 162), and one task. The task calls one allow-listed worker op on src/gobby/agents/terminal_delivery.py::deliver_existing_terminal_run, bound to the worker's database, run manager, completion_registry and run_db. That is the call cancel_agent_run makes after its commit (src/gobby/servers/routes/agents.py:807-824). After each call the task rereads the run's completion_subscribers rows, a shared table (D19), and acts on what it finds. (a) No rows left acknowledges the run. (b) A false return, meaning the run is missing or not terminal, drops it with a warning. (c) A failed call, a lost reply, a retained row or a failed reread keeps the run, and the task calls again 5 seconds later. A lost reply is an unknown outcome that the reread reconciles, never a blind retry (R0 1.3). The task calls nothing before R3's agents recovery step has finished. A gdaemon restart drops the set, and the fresh worker's startup recovery redelivers the hub machine's runs (src/gobby/runner_lifecycle_agents.py::_cleanup_terminal_agent_completion_subscribers, R3's agents step). Every native terminal transition calls deliver_completion once, after its commit and its parent delivery, even when the parent delivery fails. Those transitions are AG-1's spawn failures; AG-2's cancel, kill, stop, end, unregister, cancel_stale_helpers, cleanup, watchdog and pane-monitor terminations; and the terminations other native families make through AG-2's termination service (HOOK-2's session end and its binding of RULE-1B's step-workflow completion, PIPE-2's agent steps, CHAT-2's continue_in_chat kill and NODEHUB's node-run routes and reconciler). AG-2 builds the native in-memory completion waiters that PIPE-2's wait steps use from CP-WAVE4-CUT. deliver_completion and PIPE-2's execution completions notify them in process. A waiter also resolves from its durable agent_runs or pipeline execution row, which it reads when it registers and every 5 seconds while it waits, because Python settles remote runs (the reconcile op) and exited panes (src/gobby/agents/terminal_cleanup.py:105) until CP-WAVE5-CUT. Durable completion_subscribers delivery for agent runs keeps one owner, Python's registry, until AG-WAIT's activation (CP-WAVE5-CUT). A pipeline execution that PIPE-2 runs from CP-WAVE4-CUT has no Python producer, so PIPE-2 delivers that execution's own subscriber rows natively. At that activation deliver_completion re-binds to the native completion service and the op is no longer called. S3-DELETE deletes the op. AG-2's parked check reads the durable rows and, through one more one-line op on CompletionEventRegistry.is_awaiting, Python's in-memory subscribers, until AG-WAIT's service answers it at that activation. A transition with a composed result, such as AG-2's end_agent_run and watchdog (src/gobby/agents/run_completion.py:172-208; src/gobby/mcp_proxy/tools/agents_termination.py:114-127; src/gobby/agents/watchdog/recovery.py:770-780) or the step-workflow completion (src/gobby/workflows/engine/enforcement_completion.py:279-285), passes it to deliver_completion, because deliver_existing_terminal_run rebuilds only status, run_id and error (src/gobby/agents/terminal_delivery.py:566-598), while the subscriber's message and metadata read signoff_message and the other fields (src/gobby/events/wake_notifications.py:70-108; src/gobby/hooks/pending_messages.py:197; src/gobby/mcp_proxy/tools/agent_messaging.py:83-87). The set keeps that result with the message, and for such a run the task calls one more one-line op on deliver_and_cleanup_terminal_run (terminal_delivery.py:418-484), bound to the worker's database, completion_registry and run_db, with the same reread. A restart drops the result with the set, and startup redelivery rebuilds the plain payload, as Python's does (src/gobby/runner_lifecycle_agents.py:87-127). Task expansion's in-memory subscribers are PLANS': two one-line ops, on its subscribe helper and on CompletionEventRegistry.notify, serve them from CP-WAVE1-CUT. One caller waits on an expansion, the bundled expand-task pipeline's wait step (src/gobby/install/shared/workflows/pipelines/expand-task.yaml:60-75). Python's executor runs it against Python's own tool and registry until CP-WAVE4-CUT, and PIPE-2's step then resolves it with no op: a waiter's durable read is a function its caller passes, and PIPE-2's also answers expansion run rows through PLANS' run outcome read, because PLANS' ops reach only Python's registry. At CP-WAVE5-CUT the composed-result op and PLANS' two ops are no longer called either, and S3-DELETE deletes them.
- **rationale:** One worker op on the existing function gives the same delivery as the planned route, with no new Python. The reread is the acknowledgement, as Decision 15 rules (agents-family.md:345-390), because the helper's boolean drops the per-subscriber result. The registry is single-owner live state. Its Python callers and producers last until CP-WAVE5-CUT: wait_for_agent, remote run outcomes through the reconcile op, and the host's exit cleanup. So it moves then (D19), after PIPE-2 is native. A worker op is a call, not a long wait, so PIPE-2's waiters need a native table, and a run that Python settles reaches that table only through its durable row (src/gobby/workflows/pipeline_executor_steps.py:144-176). The composed-result op is the same delivery one level down, with one more line and no shim; re-targeting the first op at that function would move the row read and the false return into Rust and rewrite the reread that this decision rests on. CRON's feedback review op is the one long call (src/gobby/feedback/cron.py:25-28): its wait stays on Python's registry behind that call (src/gobby/feedback/agent.py:329), and native terminal transitions wake it through deliver_completion, so it needs no native waiter. The durable read takes expansion runs with one more row kind and no Python edit, where a wake from PLANS' notify would need a second binding of its seam for one wave; the cost is the 5-second recheck.

### D72: How does attention's single-owner state move while Python attention writers remain? The S2.7 plan makes Python writers clients of the native store through loopback routes (its 2.3, 4.2 and 4.3), which D4 and D19 forbid.
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default.
- **recommended_default:** The durable attention_states rows are shared rows under D19. The ordering cursor (one process epoch and seq behind one mutex, src/gobby/storage/attention.py:50-76), the in-memory metadata store (src/gobby/agents/attention_metadata.py:46-160) and event publication are single-owner live state. Python in-process writers that publish through that cursor remain until CP-WAVE5-CUT: hook ingress until CP-WAVE4-CUT (src/gobby/hooks/event_handlers/_agent.py), and four more until CP-WAVE5-CUT: the host's exit cleanup, the wake path's composer attention, the node report route and Python's handoff delivery, which stays live until then (src/gobby/agents/terminal_cleanup.py; src/gobby/terminals/composer_attention.py; src/gobby/hub/remote_pane.py:192-244; src/gobby/hooks/terminal_handoff_delivery.py; D75). So AG-3's attention family lands dormant with its own compiled Proxy default. The family is the four /api/attention/ routes, transitions, the cursor, the metadata store and publication. CP-WAVE5-CUT's activation commit flips that default, together with TERM-HOST and NODEHUB's store. Until then, native writers reach Python's AttentionStateManager.transition_async and AttentionMetadataStore.set and clear through three allow-listed worker ops that AG-2 registers as their first Rust caller. Those writers are AG-2's watchdog and pane-monitor writers from CP-WAVE2-CUT and HOOK-2's hook metadata set from CP-WAVE4-CUT. The turn lifecycle reducer is not one of them: it writes the shared rows directly and touches no cursor (D73). The Rust side stops calling the ops at CP-WAVE5-CUT, and S3-DELETE deletes them. The S2.7 plan's loopback writer routes (2.3), Python attention client (4.2), Python writer rewrites and route-override refusal (4.3) and Python deletion leaf (4.5) are not built (D4, D37). S3-DELETE deletes the Python attention surface.
- **rationale:** Two cursors would publish under two epochs. The web client refetches the roster on every epoch change and drops stale-epoch events after one resync (web/src/__tests__/attention-reconciliation.test.tsx:76, 218), so one runtime's attention updates would be lost. A native roster read under a native mutex also cannot match Python's transitions (S2.7 3.1.2). Python never calls Rust (D19), so the single owner moves after its last Python writer, and native writers call into it before then.

### D73: Who ports the turn lifecycle reducer (src/gobby/sessions/turn_lifecycle.py::TurnLifecycleReducer), and how does it write while Python's reducers and Python's attention store stay live? No plan ports it: S2.7 keeps it as a Python client of the native store until #21592's deletion leaf (its Q3 follow-up and ORCH-REV-2 item G3), the sessions plan leaves it to the hooks composition (sessions-family.md:2270-2273), s2-11 5.10 ports only the handler side, and #21592 has no plan. Yet AG-2's native pass calls it from CP-WAVE2-CUT, before any of them.
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default.
- **recommended_default:** AG-3 builds the native reducer in crates/gagents as a library that its callers run in process: begin_turn, enter_wait, resolve_wait, resumed_work, end_turn, record_provider_failure and block_provider_failure, plus get, a plain read of the shared row. Each mutation keeps Python's single transaction: it locks the session's attention_states row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, reads the session, writes the row and writes sessions.status through SES-2's status write in the same transaction, in that lock order, and makes no worker call while it holds the lock. Under D19 these are shared-row writes: Python's reducers and the native one serialize on the row lock, and the corpus proves equal row and status deltas. Before CP-WAVE5-CUT the native reducer touches no cursor and publishes nothing, as ten of Python's eleven constructions do not, because they build a private AttentionStateManager with no publisher (src/gobby/sessions/turn_lifecycle.py:284; src/gobby/hooks/event_handlers/__init__.py:118; src/gobby/servers/pending_interactions.py:76; src/gobby/servers/websocket/server.py:186-189). The eleventh, capacity recovery (src/gobby/agents/watchdog/interactive_capacity.py:38), publishes its provider-failure block today. Until CP-WAVE5-CUT that block reaches browsers on the 5-second roster refresh (web/src/hooks/useSessionAttention.ts:27, 259-261), as a hook-path provider failure does today (src/gobby/hooks/event_handlers/_misc.py:418, 498). A reducer write always leaves turn_lifecycle in the payload, so it never creates an empty row, and Python's published transitions keep running the empty-row sweep (src/gobby/storage/attention.py:491-513). From CP-WAVE5-CUT the native reducer's transitions take the native cursor and publish after commit, and the native store runs the sweep (S2.7 2.1.3 and 2.1.4; S2.7 debt, independent cursorless managers). The callers are AG-2's pass and AG-3's native terminal turn observer from CP-WAVE2-CUT, CHAT-2's pending interactions from CP-WAVE3-CUT, and HOOK-2's turn helpers and the native message processor's interrupts from CP-WAVE4-CUT, after which Python's reducer keeps two live callers until CP-WAVE5-CUT, the pending-interaction manager's Telegram question (src/gobby/servers/pending_interactions.py:136, 289) and the node report route's attention tracker (src/gobby/agents/attention_tracker.py:214, 245, through src/gobby/hub/remote_pane.py:192-244), whose writes stay safe on the row lock (D19). S3-DELETE deletes it. The observer ports src/gobby/sessions/terminal_turn_observer.py, which no plan or tree node names: TERM-1's native WS input and relay report to one turn-observer seam whose default does nothing, because Python's observer sees neither from CP-WAVE1-CUT, and from then until CP-WAVE2-CUT a mediated AGY interrupt ends its turn only on later evidence. S2.7's reducer compare-and-set with expected_payload, its status fence, bounded retry and crash repair, its waiver attention.get-roster.session-status-repair and #21592's deletion leaf are not built. Alternative: whole-method worker ops on Python's reducer until CP-WAVE5-CUT, which keep one implementation live at the cost of seven marshalled ops, a Python hop on every hook tool event from CP-WAVE4-CUT to CP-WAVE5-CUT, and two call paths in every caller.
- **rationale:** The reducer holds no live state (src/gobby/sessions/turn_lifecycle.py:277-284), so D4's worker-op clause for single-owner services does not apply and D19's shared-table rule does. A native reducer that called Python's store while holding the row lock would deadlock against _transition_locked's own lock (src/gobby/storage/attention.py:625-629). One that read plainly and sent a compare-and-set could lose an update, because transition has no expected_payload and attention_id changes only on a new episode (:558-572, 680), and adding it is a Python edit D4 does not list. S2.7 gives up atomicity only to serve a Python client of a native store, which D4 and D19 forbid, so the native reducer keeps it.

### D74: AG-2's native watchdog takes over the idle reprompt and the capacity reprompt at CP-WAVE2-CUT. Both hold Python's per-terminal composer lock across their probe, drain and write (src/gobby/agents/watchdog/recovery.py:363-399; src/gobby/agents/watchdog/interactive_capacity.py:89-111). It is the lock composer_action_lock wraps, and every Python composer writer shares it (src/gobby/terminals/composer_lock.py:10-12, 71; src/gobby/events/wake.py:860) until TERM-HOST moves it at CP-WAVE5-CUT. A lock a Python task holds cannot span separate worker ops, and run_sequence holds only the lease lock for one call (src/gobby/terminals/write_coordinator.py:265-344). How do the native reprompts keep that atomicity until then?
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default. Needs Josh's word at map approval: it adds a Python worker op beyond D4's list.
- **recommended_default:** One allow-listed worker op that AG-2 registers as its Rust caller, composer_locked_write(terminal_id, provider, gate, phases), with a small shim in R0's worker package bound to the worker's write coordinator; the shim is why it does not fit D4's one-line clause. The lock is an asyncio lock (src/gobby/terminals/write_coordinator.py:188), so the shim runs on the event loop that owns that coordinator, as TERM-1's host-effect ops do. Under the terminal's composer lock, the shim refuses with the composer state when gate is set and read_composer's state is not empty or held (interactive_capacity.py:92). It then runs the ordered phases. A phase has an action key and steps that are text, a key or the drain (composer_drain_keys, src/gobby/terminals/composer_ledger.py:602-612), sent with origin automatic as one write or one run_sequence (recovery.py:247-280), an optional observe_resolved_async key called first (recovery.py:389), and an optional interrupt action key for a failed drain: the shim checks liveness, writes Ctrl-C and Enter under that key and checks liveness again, as recovery.py:283-308 does, and only a failure there ends the run. Any other failed phase ends the run. The op returns the refusal or each phase's outcome. The idle reprompt runs its gate before the op, as Python's does (recovery.py:326), and passes two phases, clear and send. The capacity reprompt sets gate and passes one phase: drain, text and Enter (interactive_capacity.py:157-199). A failed call or a lost reply counts as an undelivered reprompt under the same bounds (recovery.py:338-344; interactive_capacity.py:118-120), and the next pass reads the composer again, so nothing is blindly retried. Two capacity steps that Python runs under the lock run outside it. The pass rereads the transcript just before the op (interactive_capacity.py:107-110), so an agent that recovers while the op waits for the lock can still get that one reprompt. It makes a refusal's blocked transition through AG-2's attention op after the op returns (interactive_capacity.py:93-105), so a composer that changes in that gap leaves a blocked entry until the next pass rereads the composer. AG-2 lands the op dormant, CP-WAVE2-CUT's activation commit starts calling it, CP-WAVE5-CUT's stops calling it when TERM-HOST re-binds the effect to gterminals' action hold (crates/gterminals/src/write_api.rs), and S3-DELETE deletes it with R0's worker package. Alternative with no Python edit: the reprompts use TERM-1's write op and the composer-read op with no lock, and CP-WAVE2-REVIEW's packet records the race as a known regression until CP-WAVE5-CUT: a reprompt's drain can wipe text a Python wake has just staged, so that wake waits for its next replay, and a reprompt can type into it.
- **rationale:** Python's wake holds the lock across its probe and write (src/gobby/events/wake.py:860) until the native decision replaces it at CP-WAVE5-CUT, and from CP-WAVE2-CUT the reprompts would otherwise be composer writers outside it, so the composer_lock.py rule that every writer shares the lock would stop holding. TERM-1's Rust action hold cannot help, because Python's coordinator stays the host's writer until TERM-HOST and Python never calls Rust (D19). Leaving the two steps in Python needs a loop R4 keeps off in worker mode and would split the idle decision's state from its write. The shim holds no state of its own and goes away with the worker package.

### D76: s2-11 ports Python's ast-based parsing (2.6's inline-interpreter classifiers, 2.8's provider-launch guard for inline scripts and 2.9's condition language) and Jinja rendering (2.13's rule templates) with crates that Cargo.lock does not have. s2-11 names rustpython-parser, and minijinja with minijinja-contrib's pycompat unknown-method callback. May the rules crate take a Python parser and those Jinja crates, and which parser?
- **status:** Default. Josh confirms it at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** Yes, with ruff_python_parser as the parser. Each is exact-pinned at its newest release that is at least two weeks old when its first consumer starts (RULE-N2 for ruff_python_parser, RULE-1B for minijinja and minijinja-contrib), only in the rules crate, after a licence and maintenance check, as D8 places hdbscan and kdtree in the memory crate. The rules crate sets its own rust-version if the pinned parser needs more than the workspace's 1.88 floor. RULE-N2 wraps ruff_python_parser in one module that exposes module and expression parsing, which the inline-interpreter classifiers, the launch guard and RULE-1H's condition parser share. RULE-N2's corpus proves the choice before anything else builds on it. RULE-1B renders with minijinja and the pycompat callback (for .get and .values), registering shlex_quote on shlex and regex_search and regex_replace on RULE-N2's pattern compiler; RULE-2's validator reuses both. If Josh declines, RULE-N2 and RULE-1H hand-write a parser for the Python expression and statement subset the corpus pins and RULE-1B hand-writes a renderer for the tags, filters and mapping methods bundled templates use (set, if, elif, else and for; join, truncate, list, shlex_quote, int and tojson; .get and .values), each about 2K more Rust, and RULE-2 refuses user-authored templates outside that subset at create and update, recorded as a contract change, as D33 refuses lookaround. A further alternative keeps s2-11's rustpython-parser and accepts that newer syntax fails to parse.
- **rationale:** Python's classifiers, condition evaluator and template engine parse with ast and Jinja, so parity on the corpus needs the same grammars. s2-11 2.6, 2.9 and 2.13 rejected hand-written parsers, because the classifiers need the full statement grammar and a second expression grammar would duplicate the first; that supersedes rust-rule-evaluation 2.4's hand-written expression parser. The maintenance check this decision requires rules out s2-11's rustpython-parser: its last release is 0.4.0 from 2024-08-06, RustPython itself moved to a fork of ruff's parser, and the 2026-09-01 fix for `except A, B:` is in no release. s2-11 also rejected treating unparsed inline Python as not read-only, so a stale grammar sends valid scripts down the path it rejected. ruff_python_parser is MIT, published about weekly by Astral, and its costs are a pre-1.0 API, which the exact pin and single wrapper contain, and an AST shaped unlike Python's ast. The map treats every new crate dependency as Josh's call (D8, D33).

### D77: RULE-1A's prepared commit would rewrite the lookbehind in .gobby/workflows/rules/quiet-hours.yaml:23, the operator's 2026-11-02 block rule. A17-TEMPLATES covers behavior-preserving rewrites of bundled templates, and this file is not one. May the commit rewrite it?
- **status:** Default. Josh confirms it at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** Yes. The audit's equivalence case proves the linear form on Python's engine, the file's version is bumped and the rule's behavior does not change; the rewrite lands in RULE-1A's prepared commit in a checkpoint cut's step 6 (D33, D39). If Josh declines, he rewrites the pattern himself before CP-WAVE4-REVIEW; otherwise the row is on that packet's rejected list and D33 requires his ruling before CP-WAVE4-CUT.
- **rationale:** The native engine cannot compile the lookbehind, so without a rewrite this block rule stops blocking at CP-WAVE4-CUT. A rewrite proven by a case is the standard D33 already sets for bundled files.

### D81: How do web chat's lifecycle passes run between CP-WAVE3-CUT, which moves web chat to CHAT-2's native runtime, and CP-WAVE4-CUT, which moves the hook pipeline and rule engine (s2-11 D1)?
- **status:** Default. Needs Josh's word at map approval: it adds a Python worker op beyond D4's list.
- **recommended_default:** CHAT-2 defines its runtime's lifecycle port and binds an interim adapter over one allow-listed worker op in R0's op table. The port carries the events Python's web chat fires today. For sessions without native hook authority: SESSION_START, BEFORE_AGENT, BEFORE_TOOL, AFTER_TOOL, PERMISSION_REQUEST, PRE_COMPACT, STOP and the plan-resolution NOTIFICATION (src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_session_launch.py:33, 49-50, 106-133, 308-312; src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_stream_events.py:87-99, 458-464; src/gobby/servers/websocket/handlers/plan_approval.py:83-95), because an AGY session's own ghook already sends its hooks to POST /api/hooks/execute. For every session, AGY's included: SESSION_END, INTERRUPT and the ask-user and tool-approval NOTIFICATION (src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_session.py:771; src/gobby/servers/websocket/handlers/session_lifecycle.py:59-72; src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_interaction_responses.py:46-80). A shim in R0's worker package rebuilds the HookEvent from the session fields and event data the runtime sends (src/gobby/hooks/events.py:122-123) and runs the whole pass that ChatLifecycleMixin._fire_lifecycle runs today (src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_lifecycle.py:119-656): the rule pass through the same WorkflowHookHandler that the hook route uses, under run_db and, for BEFORE_AGENT, worker_staging_scope (:245-255), so its passes serialize per session with the hook route's (s2-11 DR6); then blocking webhooks, metadata mcp_calls with enforcement off, event handlers, the pending-message piggyback, the broadcast over Python's existing WS bridge and non-blocking webhooks (:426-435, 497-656). It returns the pass's result plus BEFORE_AGENT's staged payload and pending message ids, and a second call of the same op, when the runtime reports the prompt delivered, commits the staged payload as a hook receipt and applies its variable effects in one transaction, only for the winner of the receipt's acknowledgment, where a failed variable write rolls the acknowledgment back and raises so that the next delivery applies both again, and marks those messages delivered after that commit (src/gobby/hooks/replay_decision.py:20-102; src/gobby/hooks/receipt_effects.py:166-225; src/gobby/servers/websocket/chat/_lifecycle.py:437-481). The native runtime applies the returned result, sends the block reply and holds the prompt-delivery reservation, including its clearing on a context reset (:147-166), because the Python mixin no longer owns the session. Failures keep Python's branches: inside the pass a BEFORE_TOOL rule failure blocks for safety (:258-281), and an evaluation timeout or any later failure returns no decision unless a BEFORE_TOOL carries git operation roots, which blocks (:484-495). An op call that itself fails or times out blocks a BEFORE_TOOL and returns no decision for any other event. CHAT-2 lands the op dormant, and CP-WAVE3-CUT's activation commit binds the adapter with the runtime. HOOK-3 implements the port on HOOK-1's manager and HOOK-2's handlers over the shared driver, so one session's web chat, hook and tool-call passes join one FIFO (s2-11 7.1, D1.1, D1.2), and CP-WAVE4-CUT's activation commit re-binds it with the hook and tool-call rule passes (D27); the Rust side then no longer calls the op, and S3-DELETE deletes it. In each window one engine owns every pass of a web chat session, Python's until CP-WAVE4-CUT and the native one after, so s2-11 7.14's Python guard is not built, and from CP-WAVE4-CUT no web chat event runs a Python rule pass for any session. The op's request takes R0's domain-op bound, not the 65,536-byte construction bound, because it carries whole tool arguments and outputs.
- **rationale:** CHAT-2 activates at CP-WAVE3-CUT, but the native pipeline (HOOK-1, HOOK-2) lands after CP-WAVE3-REVIEW and serves only from CP-WAVE4-CUT, so landing all of D1 in CHAT-2 would leave native web chat with no rule pass, webhooks, mcp_calls or event handlers for a whole wave, BEFORE_TOOL blocks included, while CP-WAVE3-CUT keeps rule evaluation in Python until HOOK-3. No existing endpoint serves the pass: it is a method of the chat mixin whose sessions CHAT-2 takes over, and POST /api/hooks/execute selects a CLI adapter by source (s2-11 4.1.2). The op holds no live state, because the rule engine, webhooks and handlers are the services the hook route uses until CP-WAVE4-CUT. AGY's three web-chat-fired events keep their pass, as today, where s2-11's guard would have dropped them until D1 (s2-11:89-92), and Python-hosted web chat never runs its passes in two engines (s2-11:93-98). As with D41, the op does not fit D4's one-line worker-op clause, because its shim rebuilds the event, so D4 lists it by name. Fallback, with no Python edit: CHAT-2's runtime activates at CP-WAVE4-CUT, where HOOK-3 binds the native port, and the activations that need native chat move with it: #25111's providers flip (AI plan 6.3), VOICE's default with GET /api/llm/status (D50), and PROJ-2's attachment relocation and namespace cutover (#25050, #25051), so CP-WAVE4-CUT's window, already the hot path's, carries all of them.

### D82: Who runs the after-tool rule pass for gateway-served tool calls from CP-MCP-CUT until CP-WAVE4-CUT (s2-11 D3)?
- **status:** Default. Needs Josh's word at map approval: it extends GW-2's worker op beyond D4's list.
- **recommended_default:** GW-2's preflight worker op also carries the after phase, in the same op entry. The gateway calls it before either leg, as D26 has it, and once more after a dispatched call completes, with the completed result; a call the before phase denies runs no after phase. A shim in R0's worker package rebuilds the completion event from the fields the before call returned, because the event is a plain dataclass with no serializer (src/gobby/hooks/events.py:122-123), and runs apply_after_tool_workflow (src/gobby/mcp_proxy/services/result_handling.py:234-287), including the direct-completion mark that the hook pipeline's after pass dedupes against (:279-287), beside the before phase's pending-context check (:150-175). An after-phase failure records diagnostics and returns the handler's result unchanged, with no redispatch (docs/contracts/internal-mcp.md:69-71; .gobby/plans/rust-internal-mcp-servers.md:60-69). CP-WAVE4-CUT's activation commit stops both phases with HOOK-3's flip (D27), and S3-DELETE deletes the op. The op's request takes R0's domain-op bound, not the 65,536-byte construction bound, because it carries whole tool arguments and outputs. The op's shim also runs the outcome tracker (D99), and each op call carries the REST request's CLI-internal marker, which the shim sets for the rule events' metadata (src/gobby/mcp_proxy/services/result_handling.py:45, 88).
- **rationale:** The contract's single policy pass is a before pass and an after pass (docs/contracts/internal-mcp.md:69-71), and s2-11 gives the gateway every before- and after-tool pass (s2-11:264). The map named only the preflight, and the compatibility endpoint runs no pass (D26), so from CP-MCP-CUT a gateway-served call would lose Python's after pass until CP-WAVE4-CUT: the after_tool rules that read a tool's output (for example src/gobby/install/shared/workflows/rules/task-enforcement/track-task-claim.yaml) for callers whose CLI runs no after-tool hook for the call, such as a REST tool call under an agent token, which Python's route enforces (src/gobby/servers/routes/mcp/endpoints/execution.py:50-57), and the step-workflow completion mark. Progressive discovery's lease tracking is not at stake, because the gateway's meta-tools write the session variables and schema leases natively (.gobby/plans/rust-internal-mcp-servers.md:69-71). The after phase needs the event the before phase built, so it needs a shim, and D4 lists it by name, as D41 does. ### D86: client-operator-verbs 1.5 and 1.7 (#21571) plan a command inventory (docs/contracts/cli-inventory.toml, checked by tests/cli/test_cli_inventory.py over gobby.cli.cli and by crates/gclient/tests/cli_inventory.rs) and a parity gate over it (crates/gclient/tests/operator_inventory_parity.rs), and node-mode 2.7 (plan #25258) adds a node field to every row (carried, a task ref, or hub). #21571's disposition says gport's ledger supersedes the 1.5 inventory, and no chunk defines a parity gate over it. The gate is each verb chunk's REC-CLI golden replay over its own rows (D16) plus S3-FREEZE's closure with zero rows proxied (D20), which S3-NAME follows before the client takes the gobby name. No chunk builds docs/contracts/cli-inventory.toml, tests/cli/test_cli_inventory.py, crates/gclient/tests/cli_inventory.rs or crates/gclient/tests/operator_inventory_parity.rs. A verb with no Python command has no row, so its native tests are its readiness evidence, as for D53: config get|set and lease status|promote|recover in V1A, gobby cron output in V5A, gobby node install and enroll in S4-RELEASE, and gobby node status, start, stop and restart and gobby nodes update in S4-INSTALL. node-mode 2.7's node field (whether a verb runs on a node, the task that brings it, or hub only) becomes a column of #25246's node parity inventory in S4-PROOF (docs/guides/hub-node-smoke.md), filled from executed evidence on a node. Those verbs ship in 1.0, as #21571's card and plan #25258 ask. Alternative for the lease verbs and cron output: defer them past 1.0 under D6, because operators keep gdaemon's lease routes (docs/guides/admin-operations.md:354-364) and CRON's raw-output route, and nothing else depends on them.
- **rationale:** The ledger already lists every Python command with its owner, and S3-FREEZE already refuses a proxied row before S3-NAME, which is what 1.7 gated ahead of the naming switch; a second inventory would restate the ledger and drift from it. The inventory's Python test walks gobby.cli.cli: it records no oracle, so D4 does not list it, and S3-DELETE removes the tree it walks before Stage 4 adds node verbs. #25246 already expands W01-W32 into the exact verbs available at the candidate SHA with their evidence, so the node field is one column of it. Rejected: a node column on gport's ledger, which would change P0-RECORD's ledger format for rows that only Stage 4 can fill. The lease verbs and cron output are still new capability, which D6's port-as-is rule defers by default: #23458 retired Python's gobby lease on 2026-10-11, and the cron verb is the Orchestrator's 2026-10-25 amendment on #21571. So Josh confirms them, as ruling 22 did for D53's config verb.

### D87: #24173's criteria 4-7, folded from #22340, ask for agent conversation channels on the communications core: global, project, per-spawn-tree private, direct messages and threads, with posting rules and wake defaults; delivery by hook piggyback, mention routing and a blocking wait for message with per-member read cursors; and a Plan Writer and Plan Adversary consensus protocol over a channel. Agents converse through what 1.0 ports: COMMS-1's and COMMS-2's channels over D28's adapters, AG-3's mailbox with send_message's session, parent, agent, project and global targets, HOOK-2's piggyback of pending messages (s2-11 5.9) and AG-WAIT's wait_for_coordination. These are not built: agent_channels and .gobby/plans/gobby-messaging.md's migrations 460-462, crates/gmsg, /api/messaging, read_channel, post_message, set_subscription, wait_for_message, get_consensus, per-member read cursors, mention routing and the consensus protocol. #24173's criteria 4-6 close unmet under this decision, and its criterion 8 is AG-3's (D29). Alternative: a post-1.0 task builds native channels on AG-3's mailbox; nothing in 1.0 blocks it, and COMMS-1's adapter contract does not change for it.
- **rationale:** Josh, 2026-10-27, on the fold: 'gobby-comms is required, which will give us slack access and will satisfy this'. Python serves none of these surfaces, so no ledger row selects them and no corpus records them, and port-as-is defers new capability (D6). #22340 has been parked since Josh's 2026-10-05 'Gobby messaging should be deferred', and rulings 1 and 5 retire plan files and Adversary stamps for port work, so the consensus protocol has no 1.0 consumer. The cost is that agents get no threaded private channel in 1.0 beyond what send_message and the comms channels carry today.

### D60: Under the Homebrew distribution, where do gdaemon and gmcp come from once CP-PREDELETE-CUT's commit B makes GobbyAI/homebrew-tap's gobby formula install the Rust client (D55)? A Homebrew install has neither today: install provisions gdaemon unconditionally but only from a Gobby workspace build with cargo on PATH (src/gobby/cli/install_setup.py:141-146; src/gobby/cli/install_setup_gdaemon.py:134-138; src/gobby/install/bin_set_coherence.py:37-42), and under Homebrew it verifies only the gcode, ghook, gterm and gclient helper formulae and skips the managed binary installs, gmcp's included (src/gobby/install/distribution.py:18-24, 49-55; src/gobby/cli/install_setup.py:189-207, 291-331). S3-NAME drops gclient from that helper list, and S3-DELETE removes the Python install. #24359's card answers only for gmcp, with a gobby-mcp formula and a Homebrew helper-list entry, and leaves gdaemon without a source.
- **status:** Default. Josh confirms it at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** One formula carries the set. The gobby formula installs the client archive (D55) plus Homebrew resources for gdaemon, gcode, ghook, gterm and gmcp, taken from the release archives of their own workflows (.github/workflows/release-gdaemon.yml, .github/workflows/release-gcode.yml, .github/workflows/release-ghook.yml, .github/workflows/release-gterminal.yml, .github/workflows/release-gmcp.yml) at the versions the client's tagged commit names in its crate manifests, with nothing rebuilt, as .gobby/plans/node-install-enrollment.md D1 assembles a node bundle. One version names one source under the release guard, so gcode, gdaemon and ghook, the stamped coherent set, stay coherent, and the tap's four helper formulae, gobby-code, gobby-hooks, gobby-local and gobby-squeeze, retire (D127); the gobby-terminal and gobby-client names in src/gobby/install/distribution.py:19-24 were never formulae in the tap. No workflow in this repository changes for this: the moved tap dispatch's tag and gobby_repo let the tap read those manifests (.github/workflows/release.yml:116-158). S3-NAME's Rust change makes V1B's Homebrew helper check verify those five binaries against the client's version pins, with gobby named as the formula to install or upgrade for each, in place of the four formula names it checks today, and under the Homebrew distribution the install verb verifies gdaemon through that check instead of provisioning it from a workspace build. Under this default #24359 adds neither a gobby-mcp formula nor a helper-list entry. Outside this repository, GobbyAI/homebrew-tap takes the formula change together with D55's switch to the client, through the pull request D127 names, and its update job waits until every member's archive at those versions exists before it changes the formula, because the client's tag and dispatch come before gterm's and gdaemon's releases in the publication order (.gobby/plans/node-install-enrollment.md E1 gate 3). Today no member has a release at its pinned version: the repository's tags stop at gcode-v1.5.0 and ghook-v0.7.2, with no gdaemon-v*, gterm-v* or gmcp-v* tag, against the pins in src/gobby/install/version_pins.py:5-15. Josh's publication at that gate is the first that has them (#24359's ruling of 2026-10-13 holds gmcp's tag for his authorization), so until then a Homebrew gobby stays unable to run a daemon, as it is today. Alternative: keep one formula per binary, add gobby-daemon and gobby-mcp formulae from the gdaemon-v* and gmcp-v* releases (.github/workflows/release-gdaemon.yml, .github/workflows/release-gmcp.yml), gobby-mcp being the formula #24359's card names, and have the check name gdaemon and gmcp beside gcode, ghook and gterm; each formula then moves on its own tag, so the check's version floors are the only guard on the coherent set.
- **rationale:** Without gdaemon a Homebrew gobby cannot start a daemon; that is already true and stays true after S3-DELETE unless the formula supplies it. gcode, gdaemon and ghook share one schema identity, which separately tagged formulae can break by upgrading one member alone, while one formula whose resources move together keeps the set coherent and changes only the helper list in this repository. S4-RELEASE's node bundle would carry the same members, but it exists only on a gdaemon-v* release from S4-RELEASE's landing on, so the formula takes the members' own archives. The tap lives outside this repository, so Josh decides its shape.

### D61: S3-DELETE removes pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and with them every dependency CVE audit in the repository: ci.yml's security job runs bandit and uv audit (.github/workflows/ci.yml:467-494), .github/workflows/dependency-audit.yml runs uv audit monthly and on demand (.github/workflows/dependency-audit.yml:3-6, 18-32), and the pre-push hook and both pre-push scripts run pip-audit (.pre-commit-config.yaml:94-101; pre-push-test.sh:517-530; pre-push-test-short.sh:131-141). ### D63: Projects plan 4.6's journal turns on at CP-FINAL-CUT (D47), and plan 4.5a requires every project.json policy reader to refuse pending recovery evidence rather than read a candidate that SQL has not committed. 4.5a integrates that guard only in the Python consumers D47 does not build, and no chunk says what the native readers outside gprojects do. Which readers take it, where does it live, and what proves it before the flip?
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default.
- **recommended_default:** One guard in gcore, landed by PROJ-1 (crates/gcore/src/project_metadata.rs): it opens .gobby/.project.json.lock as 4.5a specifies, takes the exclusive flock within at most two seconds, checks .gobby/.project-update-recovery/ under the lock, and returns the committed object, absent metadata, or a distinct refusal for malformed or non-object metadata, an unreadable file, a lock deadline or pending evidence. No caller turns a refusal into missing metadata, empty rules, absent verification or a default policy (.gobby/plans/gdaemon-projects-files-docs-family.md:1010-1014). It is synchronous, and async callers run it off the executor (:1008). A caller reads in one call or keeps the returned guard held across its merge and publication, passes a held guard to nested helpers instead of locking twice (:1030-1031), and takes it before any project row lock, never while holding one (:1016-1017). PROJ-2's metadata_lock.rs, 4.6's publication service and read.rs hold the same guard and resolve a journal, and update_recovery joins R3's startup order on either default, so an entry that process loss left does not keep other readers refusing until the next projects-family read. Every native policy reader outside gprojects reads through it from its own landing, with a boundary test that seeds a pending entry: B0-WRITE (#25506's task protection policy), B0-CLOSE (task_protection_policy_unavailable), SRC (merge verification), PLANS (expansion's verification commands), AG-1 (launch's sandbox write paths and metadata copy, crates/gdaemon/src/nodes/agents/sandbox/caches.rs:204-215 and crates/gdaemon/src/nodes/agents/repair.rs:135-143), AG-4 (the worktree and clone metadata copy), CHAT-2 (chat approval and the Codex and Droid permission callbacks), RULE-1H (the stop gate's verification commands and transcript evidence), HOOK-3 (hold-open autoapproval) and V5A (hooks status, run, enable and disable; enable and disable also merge under the guard). Two classes are exempt by name: identity reads of id or project_id (crates/gcore/src/project.rs:52-77, gcode, crates/gmcp/src/daemon.rs:191; plan :986-987), and ghook's hooks_disabled read (crates/ghook/src/dispatch.rs:363-369). CP-FINAL-CUT's step 3 seat reviews a literal search of crates/ before the flip. Alternative: build the reader in gprojects, as 4.5a's targets list it, so that PROJ-2's landing edits the B0, SRC and PLANS crates and those crates and the CLI take a gprojects dependency.
- **rationale:** B0-WRITE, B0-CLOSE, SRC and PLANS land before PROJ-2, and PROJ-2 already reaches B0-WRITE and B0-CLOSE through CP-TEMPLATE-CUT, so those two cannot depend on it and SRC and PLANS would need a new edge to it, while every reader already reaches PROJ-1. Families reach each other only through public APIs and Cargo rejects a cycle (crates/AGENTS.md), gclient does not link gprojects, and the families and the CLI all link gcore, so gcore is the one home that adds no edge between families, beside crates/gcore/src/project.rs and D47's crates/gcore/src/project_fence.rs. The guard adds no trait, seam or default: it is a library call, live wherever its caller is live and removed by nothing. With no journal it only takes the flock that Python's project initialization and D64's policy writers already take, so it is harmless before CP-FINAL-CUT, and guarding only behind the journal default would strand an entry that cut's rollback left. ghook is exempt because of two facts: a journaled candidate changes only the requested metadata fields and preserves every other key (plan :1142-1145), and hooks_disabled is written only by file-only merges that take no SQL transaction and refuse pending recovery (plan :1018-1019), so no pending candidate can hold an uncommitted hooks_disabled value. Any failure there already keeps hooks on, and ghook is sandbox-tolerant and runs on every hook (crates/ghook/Cargo.toml), where it may be unable to open the sidecar and a two-second wait would stall the CLI.

### D64: Python's approval and validation savers and the CLI's hook toggles rewrite project.json with unlocked, non-atomic writes today, and D47 leaves them as recorded because #25057, which would fix them, is not built. Land the fix, or keep recording the bug?
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default. Josh confirms it at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** Land it under D4's bug-fix clause (rulings 6 and 15), as its own commit with its test, in REC-PLATFORM before that chunk records the project routes, unless 0.9.0 already carries the fix; the friction queue (#25603) may land it sooner. The commit does four things and takes nothing else from #25057. (1) src/gobby/servers/tool_approvals.py's save, migrate and clear, src/gobby/config/validation_detection.py's save, which its clear calls, and src/gobby/cli/extensions.py's hooks disable and enable publish the same serialized JSON through src/gobby/utils/durable_file.py's durable_replace_text with the file's existing mode (:79-115, :175-177), whose temp file, fsync, os.replace, directory fsync and readback also close the crash case. (2) Those writers, src/gobby/project_verification/refresh.py's _write_verification (:198-220) and src/gobby/utils/project_init.py's update_project_json_fields (:606-637), which are atomic but unlocked, hold durable_file.exclusive_file_lock on project.json with a two-second deadline across read, merge and publication. (3) The savers' read-for-merge refuses malformed, non-object or unreadable JSON, keeping the file's bytes and mode, instead of substituting an empty payload (src/gobby/servers/tool_approvals.py:300-315; src/gobby/config/validation_detection.py:949-957; Projects plan 4.5a.4); _write_verification keeps its own backup-and-repair contract (.gobby/plans/gdaemon-projects-files-docs-family.md:1026-1028, 1150). (4) PUT and PATCH /api/projects/{project_id} answer those refusals with 4.6's 422 and 503 bodies (plan :1147-1149). Readers and the chat, hook and task consumers stay as they are (D47). Narrower alternative: parts (1) to (3) only, so the routes answer a refusal with their existing error, REC-PLATFORM records that, and #25058's two metadata-refusal waiver entries land in CP-WAVE1-CUT's activation commit, the flip that serves 4.6's bodies. Alternative: keep the bug as recorded until its callers go: REC-PLATFORM records it, those two entries land the same way, a malformed file keeps losing its other keys until CP-WAVE1-CUT, and the CLI's toggles keep racing until CP-PREDELETE-CUT. S3-DELETE deletes this fix with the rest of src/gobby.
- **rationale:** Confirmed from source: project_file.write_text (src/gobby/servers/tool_approvals.py:346, 370-373, 394-397; src/gobby/config/validation_detection.py:312) and open(path, 'w') (src/gobby/cli/extensions.py:463-464, 499-500) truncate in place with no lock. The two savers, reached from src/gobby/servers/routes/projects.py:510 and :514, and the CLI's toggles are the live paths; the approval migrate and clear helpers and the validation clear helper have no caller in src or tests and take the same fix, so that no truncating writer stays in those modules. A concurrent reader (ghook on every hook, gcore's read_project_id, gcode, Python's get_project_context) can see an empty or partial file, a crash leaves the file truncated, concurrent writers lose updates, and the empty-payload substitution overwrites a malformed file, for example one with merge-conflict markers in the tracked .gobby/project.json, with only the policy key, which loses the project id. This is live on 0.9.0 (ruling 15): PUT and PATCH serve on Python until CP-WAVE1-CUT and the CLI's toggles until CP-PREDELETE-CUT, so it is a bug fix and not the hardening D47 defers. D47's conclusion stands, because Python's update order and its lock-free readers remain. REC-PLATFORM is the chunk because landing the fix before recording needs no D18 re-record and native 4.6's contract then matches the recording; landing it in PROJ-2 would leave it live only from that chunk's prepared commit to CP-WAVE1-CUT's flip and force a re-record. The fix needs some refusal for malformed or unreadable metadata, and using 4.6's 422 and 503 bodies gives one contract instead of two and retires #25058's two metadata-refusal entries, so this is not an edit that only aligns Python with the native contract, which A1-SECRETS' rule excludes. A refusal raises inside apply_update's transaction (src/gobby/servers/routes/projects.py:499-516), so the row update rolls back. That save takes the flock inside the transaction, the reverse of plan 4.5a's lock order (:1016-1017), and the two-second deadline bounds the wait and answers 503; no native update runs beside it, because PUT and PATCH leave Python at CP-WAVE1-CUT's flip. A landing through the friction queue changes nothing here, because this chunk records whatever 0.9.0 then does. update_project_json_fields joins the locked set although it is atomic, because project initialization reaches it (src/gobby/utils/project_init.py:325) and a stale merge there would drop a saver's key. The other project.json writers stay as they are: _update_project_json_verification has no production caller, _write_project_json only creates the file and merges nothing, and src/gobby/utils/project_context.py's isolation copies write a new checkout that no saver can name yet.

### D65: Two plan leaves edit settings editors under web/, and no cut lands either edit: gmcp-stdio 1.7 (#24356, Decision 12) retires mcp_client_proxy.tool_timeouts with its editor and route, and code-index 9.7 (#24713) removes code_index.nightly_repair_timeout_seconds and code_index.maintenance_log_file with their fields. D14 and D32 moved parts of both leaves without saying what becomes of these edits. What lands, and where?
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default. Josh confirms it at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** (1) tool_timeouts stays. Closed #24352's gmcp reads it (crates/gmcp/src/call_tool.rs:191-193; crates/gmcp/src/daemon.rs:160-189), so the setting, GET /api/mcp/bridge/tool-timeouts (MUX-1's row, which makes #21566's D5 registry 19 rows) and the settings editor stay, and #24356's 1.7.3, 1.7.6 and 1.7.7 are not built. (2) code_index.maintenance_log_file leaves in CP-FINAL-CUT's activation commit, the promotion at which its last reader goes; D32 keeps only nightly_repair_timeout_seconds. That commit removes its contract entry, its settings field and test fixture, its frozen config cases and docs, and any stored config_store row through a destructive migration (D22), and the cut runs gobby ui build through V1B's native verb after the promotion's restart. Its deactivation commit reverts all of it, and the cut runs gobby ui build again after promoting that build. (3) Every cutover's step 2 carries one sentence for any other web/ change it lands, a pick included, because web fixes are routine and D40's picks can carry them. Alternative for (1): retire the setting at S3-DELETE as the plan says, also deleting gmcp's fetch and MUX-1's route and adding the web edit to CP-FINAL-CUT's commit. Alternative for (2): keep the key through 1.0, which leaves a settings field with no reader (AGENTS.md rule 4).
- **rationale:** Decision 12's reason was that keeping the setting 'would mean porting that fetch, its cache, and its retry into gmcp, for a map that ships empty' (.gobby/plans/gmcp-stdio.md:168-177), and #24352 then ported it, so today's gmcp honors the setting and the plan's targets do not remove that code. Keeping it is port-as-is and the smaller change, and the retirement stays open after 1.0. For (2), the native jobs log to gdaemon's stderr and the key loses its last reader with the Python files (.gobby/plans/code-index-family.md:3787-3790, 3800-3801); D32's reason, a safety timeout, does not cover a log path. The removal sits in CP-FINAL-CUT's activation commit and not in S3-DELETE's, because that commit is already a schema step with drops, so its destructive DELETE of a stored row adds no new rollback cost, and its deactivation commit restores contract, field and frozen cases together, whereas S3-DELETE's commit stays in the deactivation build, beside a row that a backup restore brings back while no contract knows it. A stored key that the registry does not know is the state Python's reconcile_registry refuses (src/gobby/storage/config_repository.py:175-202), so the map leaves none behind. For (3), the daemon serves web/dist from disk, web/dist is untracked (web/.gitignore:2), and the landing policy says that gobby ui build is what activates a web/ edit (src/gobby/tasks/landing_policy.py:26-29, 63-73), so no landing or promotion can stand in for it.

### D66: The sessions plan drops gobby sessions renumber and gobby sessions backfill-context-windows as its debt B1 and B2 (.gobby/plans/sessions-family.md:326-327): renumber rewrites durable #N session references, and the backfill is a finished one-off repair. ### D67: How does a native session status write reach Python's communications manager before COMMS-2 moves the comms connections at CP-WAVE5-CUT? Sessions 2.2 (ruling C4 (a)) plans a new Python LISTEN bridge, src/gobby/storage/sessions/status_notifications.py started from SessionLifecycleManager (.gobby/plans/sessions-family.md:983-999), a Python edit D4 does not list, and AG-3's native replay already takes the bridge's other registrant.
- **status:** Default. Needs Josh's word at map approval: it adds a Python worker op beyond D4's list.
- **recommended_default:** One allow-listed worker op in R0's op table on CommunicationsManager.handle_session_status_transition (src/gobby/communications/manager.py:804-819), with a small shim in R0's worker package that rebuilds the SessionStatusTransition (src/gobby/sessions/status_events.py) from the op's payload; the shim is why it does not fit D4's one-line clause. SES-2 lands it dormant, and CP-WAVE2-CUT's activation commit registers a gdaemon listener on SES-2's committed native transitions that calls it. It never runs _notify_status_transition (src/gobby/storage/sessions/_bootstrap.py:55-79), so Python's wake replay sees only Python's writes and AG-3's native replay only native ones. A failed call logs, as Python's listener does (src/gobby/runner_broadcasting.py:439-447), and never rolls back the write. From CP-WAVE5-CUT's activation COMMS-2's native listener takes over and the Rust side stops calling the op, and S3-DELETE deletes it. Alternative with no Python edit: no op. The operator-target drain still runs from Python's polling and inbound paths (src/gobby/communications/polling.py:117; src/gobby/communications/inbound.py:327). What is lost is fallback_telegram_targets (src/gobby/communications/manager.py:816-819) for a native write to a non-live status: the Telegram target stays on the ended session until a restart's restore reconcile (src/gobby/communications/manager.py:176-213) or CP-WAVE5-CUT, and CP-WAVE2-REVIEW's packet records that as a known regression.
- **rationale:** Python's only status listeners are wake replay and session status communications (src/gobby/events/wake_recovery.py:47; src/gobby/runner_broadcasting.py:451). Python never calls Rust (D19) and the connections stay Python's until COMMS-2, so the call goes from Rust into Python. From CP-WAVE4-CUT every hook-driven session end is a native write, so the alternative's regression would cover all of them until CP-WAVE5-CUT. The op goes away with the rest at S3-DELETE, where a LISTEN bridge would add a Python service and a lifecycle edit.

### D68: What serves POST /api/admin/restart, POST /api/admin/shutdown and POST /api/admin/lease/handoff once gdaemon is the runner, what admits a caller there, and how is a session cookie verified before SEAM-CALLERS' verifier is live? The ledger shows the rows proxied with owner R6, and R6 and CP-RUNNER-CUT do not reach SEAM-CALLERS.
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default. It puts a stop authority behind an interim cookie check, so Josh gives his word at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** The rows go Native in CP-RUNNER-CUT's activation commit, on the compiled default that flips the runner, with exact POST claims. After the front door's authenticate, R6 admits in a fixed order: a gobby-agent-v1. bearer is refused by presence (403 managed_activation_refused on restart and shutdown, 401 route_not_permitted on lease handoff, as Python answers a live token), then an API key or a loopback break-glass is an operator, then a browser-testing. cookie is refused, then any other session cookie is checked by sending only that cookie to Python's existing GET /api/auth/status, and anything else answers 401 missing_auth. AUTH re-binds the cookie port to SEAM-CALLERS' verifier at CP-WAVE1-CUT's activation, with the shared CORS layer, and S3-DELETE removes the adapter. Three refusals are stricter than Python and are accepted differences with native tests instead of recorded cases: a dead, forged or identity-mismatched agent bearer (Python answers its own 401 reason), an agent bearer with a valid break-glass header (Python admits it, src/gobby/servers/auth_service.py:483-484) and a dead browser-testing. cookie (Python answers 401). Restart's start proof stays Python's through one R6 worker op until CP-WAVE5-CUT's activation commit re-binds it to a Rust proof that R6 builds and V1A reuses. That proof leaves out Python's worktree, dirty-content and pin steps and verifies the SRT runner without restaging it, for the reasons R6's goal gives, and those are accepted differences too. Once CP-PREDELETE-CUT's commit A leaves no worker, restart runs the whole ordered stop and gdaemon re-executes itself, with a null backend_pid. Alternatives: the rows stay proxied until CP-MCP-CUT, the first cut that reaches SEAM-CALLERS, with a Rust watcher on the marker or a long-poll worker op; R6 takes the verifier; key-only admission; a Rust start proof from CP-RUNNER-CUT with no op. S3-DELETE deletes the restart start-proof entry with the worker package.
- **rationale:** A proxied row cannot stay under the Rust runner: Python's routes only write the marker and set flags with no reader (src/gobby/runner_lifecycle.py:315-319), and exiting the worker on them would skip R6's ordered stop. A marker watcher also fires on the marker's CLI writers, which precede a signal (src/gobby/cli/utils_shutdown.py:149; src/gobby/cli/installers/service.py:598, 646), it adds a second stop path, and Python's protected-run read goes blind at CP-WAVE1-CUT (src/gobby/scheduler/scheduler.py:120-130). R6 taking the verifier would move #24967 and its security review ahead of the first cut or write a second verifier (D3, #25068). Key-only admission breaks the web UI's restart command (web/src/lib/api.ts:93; web/src/components/app/useAppCommandPalette.ts:85). Python's own status route is the existing verifier: it answers from validate_session alone for such a cookie (src/gobby/servers/routes/auth.py:194-198; src/gobby/servers/auth_service.py:659-665), under D19 with no Python edit. The presence refusal needs no token verifier at all, so no agent token can reach a stop whatever the state of SEAM-CALLERS. A worker op on validate_session would be more mechanism than the existing endpoint. The start proof has two bindings because a restart cannot skip it, since a worker's boot refusal is sticky (crates/gdaemon/src/state.rs:245-253), and because S3-FREEZE asserts zero worker ops after CP-WAVE5-CUT, which V1A cannot feed. A Rust proof from CP-RUNNER-CUT would need the worker's source root, which gdaemon does not hold (crates/gdaemon/src/lifecycle/backend.rs:85-109), a new handshake field to get it, Rust ports of the dirty-content check and the SRT restage, and the sandbox flags before A1-CONFIG, all to replace one call to Python's own proof.

### D69: How do gclient's gobby sync and gobby install's content step reach the hub? Python writes the DB directly (src/gobby/cli/sync.py:212-216; src/gobby/cli/install_setup.py:140-165). D16 says a verb with no endpoint adds one through Found Work, gclient links no PostgreSQL driver (crates/gclient/Cargo.toml), and both verbs must work with no daemon running.
- **resolved_by:** None
- **status:** Default. It settles how the rule that clients do not mutate the DB applies to install and sync, so Josh gives his word at map approval.
- **recommended_default:** gclient stays free of any datastore connection and execs gdaemon content-sync with inherited stdio, as V5B execs gdaemon mcp-auth, resolving gdaemon from <gobby_home>/bin and then PATH. gdaemon is the schema authority, already resolves the bootstrap's database URL and embeds the template tree, so the subcommand calls the same sync as R2's content phase. V1B owns it, it lands dormant, and it ships in CP-PREDELETE-CUT's commit A. Any other verb or install step that must work with no daemon running takes the same path, such as V1A's gdaemon handoff-guard and gdaemon start-proof. Alternative: an endpoint, with install starting a daemon first.
- **rationale:** An endpoint cannot serve gobby install, which syncs before any daemon has started, or gobby sync with the daemon stopped (src/gobby/cli/sync.py:58-90), and an HTTP hard delete for --reinstall would add an admission surface to a route family that has none. Adding a datastore driver to gclient would make the client mutate the DB. gdaemon's subcommands already write the hub (gdaemon schema apply; MUX-1's mcp-auth), so no new kind of writer appears.

### D70: The app lifespan expires every pending interaction row on each start (src/gobby/servers/_app_lifecycle.py:110-121; src/gobby/servers/pending_interactions.py:385-420), so from CP-WAVE3-CUT a plain restart's new worker would expire CHAT-2's live rows. The edit is dormant until CP-RUNNER-CUT: with its entry on, or without the worker marker, the expire runs as it does today. CP-WAVE3-CUT's activation takes the entry off when CHAT-2's expire pass takes over, and S3-DELETE deletes the file. Alternative needing no edit to that file: the worker package replaces the manager's expire at boot, which hides the gate from anyone reading the lifespan.
